topicTitle: NEB Class 11 Chemistry — Classification of Elements — 2024
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: What is the modern periodic law? Explain how it improved on Mendeleev's periodic law.
questions.solution:
**Modern periodic law:** properties of elements are periodic functions of their **atomic numbers**.

It fixed Mendeleev (atomic-mass) defects: (1) anomalous pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni) fall in correct order; (2) no unexplained gaps remain — all 118 elements placed; (3) noble gases get a natural group without disturbing the table.
questions.knowledgeNote: Moseley (1913) and X-ray spectra moved the table from mass to atomic number.
questions.answer: **Modern periodic law:** element properties are a periodic function of **atomic number**. **Improvements on Mendeleev (mass-based):** (1) anomalous pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni, Te/I) fall into correct groups with no inversions; (2) isotopes (same Z, different mass) share one position; (3) the table gains an electronic foundation — periods/groups/blocks follow directly from electron configuration, which atomic number determines. **Deep point:** mass misordered three pairs and every isotope; atomic number fixes all four with one change of basis.

questions.question: What are s-, p-, d-, and f-blocks? Give one element belonging to each.
questions.solution:
Blocks named by the subshell receiving the last electron: **s-block** — Na; **p-block** — Cl; **d-block** (transition metals) — Fe; **f-block** (inner transition) — U.

s + p = representative elements; d = transition; f = lanthanides/actinides.
questions.knowledgeNote: Helium (1s²) sits with the p-block noble gases by behaviour, not by configuration — the famous exception.
questions.answer: **s-block:** the last electron enters an **ns** orbital — groups 1–2 (e.g. **Na**). **p-block:** the last electron enters an **np** orbital — groups 13–18 (e.g. **Cl**). **d-block:** the last electron enters a **(n−1)d** orbital — groups 3–12, the transition elements (e.g. **Fe**). **f-block:** the last electron enters a **(n−2)f** orbital — the lanthanides and actinides, placed below the main table (e.g. **Ce**). **Deep point:** the block is simply the address of the differentiating electron — the one electron that makes the element different from its predecessor.

questions.question: Define ionisation energy. Explain why nitrogen has a higher first ionisation energy than oxygen.
questions.solution:
**Ionisation energy** is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom.

N (1s² 2s² 2p³) has a **half-filled p subshell** — extra stable. Removing its electron breaks that stability, costing more energy than removing one from O (2p⁴), where repulsion between paired electrons actually helps ejection.
questions.knowledgeNote: Half-filled/full subshells (N, P, Be, Mg, noble gases) always spike above the trend — the standard 'anomaly' question.
questions.answer: **Ionisation energy (IE₁):** the minimum energy required to remove the most loosely bound electron from an isolated gaseous atom: M(g) + IE₁ → M⁺(g) + e⁻ (measured in kJ/mol). **Why N > O:** nitrogen is 2s²2p³ — the three p orbitals are **half-filled**, an exchange-energy-stabilised, symmetrical configuration; oxygen is 2s²2p⁴ — its fourth p electron is **paired**, and removing it relieves the pairing repulsion. So although O is further right (higher Zeff), the electron it loses is the easier one: IE₁(N) = 1402 > IE₁(O) = 1314 kJ/mol. **Deep point:** the N/O inversion is the same story as Be/B and Mg/Al — half-filled (or filled) stability and pairing repulsion override the period trend at exactly those two points.

questions.question: Define electronegativity. How does it vary across a period and down a group? Which element is the most electronegative?
questions.solution:
**Electronegativity** is an atom's pull on shared bond electrons.

It **increases left→right** (rising nuclear charge) and **decreases top→bottom** (larger, shielded atoms). **Fluorine (4.0)** is the maximum.
questions.knowledgeNote: Noble gases have no EN values (no bonds to pull in) — a tidy one-mark follow-up.
questions.answer: **Electronegativity:** the tendency of an atom to attract the **shared pair of electrons** toward itself in a covalent bond (Pauling scale, F = 4.0). **Across a period:** increases (left → right) — nuclear charge rises while the shell count is constant, so Zeff and the pull on shared electrons rise (Li 1.0 → F 4.0). **Down a group:** decreases — new shells enlarge the atom and screen the nucleus, so the shared pair is pulled less strongly (F 4.0 → Cs 0.7). **Most electronegative element: fluorine.** **Deep point:** electronegativity is ionisation energy and electron affinity blended into one bond-context number — its trends mirror IE's because the cause (Zeff) is shared.

questions.question: How does atomic radius vary across a period and down a group? Explain the trend in each case.
questions.solution:
**Across a period it shrinks:** added protons pull the same shell tighter.

**Down a group it grows:** each new principal shell outweighs the extra nuclear charge.
questions.knowledgeNote: Cations < parent atom < anions — size order within one element's ions.
questions.answer: **Across a period:** the atomic radius **decreases** — nuclear charge (Z) rises while electrons enter the **same shell**, so shielding stays roughly constant and Zeff pulls the shell inward (Na 186 pm → Cl 99 pm). **Down a group:** the radius **increases** — each element adds a **new shell** (higher n), whose outer electrons stand farther out and are screened by the inner shells; the added shells outweigh the rising Z (Li 152 pm → Cs 262 pm). **Deep point:** one sentence per direction — across, same shell + more protons = smaller; down, extra shell + extra shielding = bigger.

questions.question: What is diagonal relationship? Give one example with cause.
questions.solution:
Diagonally adjacent elements (e.g. **Li and Mg**) resemble each other more than their own group members.

Cause: similar charge density (charge/radius) — moving right shrinks size while moving down grows it, roughly cancelling along the diagonal. Both form nitrides, sparingly soluble carbonates, and similar organometallics.
questions.knowledgeNote: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si are the three classic diagonal pairs.
questions.answer: **Diagonal relationship:** the similarity in properties between an element and the element **diagonally down-right** of it in period 2/3 (Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si). **Example — Li and Mg:** both form nitrides directly (Li₃N, Mg₃N₂), both give normal carbonates that decompose on heating (Li₂CO₃, MgCO₃ — unlike the other alkali/alkaline-earth carbonates), both form covalent organo-compounds, similar solubilities of fluorides/phosphates. **Cause:** the diagonal pair has **similar charge/size (ionic potential)** — moving right raises charge, moving down raises size; the diagonal step raises both, leaving the charge-to-radius ratio (polarising power) nearly unchanged, so the two elements polarise anions similarly and behave alike. **Deep point:** periodicity is vertical, but ionic potential is a ratio — and the diagonal is the direction along which that ratio constant-walks.
